entries.modern_form: Semitic root b-r-k: Proto-Semitic *birk- 'knee' / West Semitic brk 'to kneel; to bless' (AHD Semitic roots brk)
entries.note: The root is real and its label 'Semitic' is right. Wiktionary reconstructs Proto-Semitic *birk- 'knee' (Akk. birkum, Heb. berekh, Ug. brk, Syr. burkā, Ge'ez bərk) with a metathetic variant *rukbat- (Ar. rukba). The 'kneel (of a camel) > bless' story is the traditional Gesenius/BDB account and matches Arabic baraka 'to kneel (camel)' / bāraka 'to bless'. The AHD Semitic appendix (Nourai's own AHD source) instead treats brk 'to bless' as 'probably a metathesized variant of krb' (Akk. karābu 'to praise, bless') — that is the hypothesis underlying Nourai's Akkadian/Hebrew cherub branch; it is accepted by AHD and Klein but rejected by recent Hebrew lexicography (SAHD, citing Mitchell: metathesis of first and third radicals is extremely rare). The griffin sub-branch is speculative (Klein) and not adopted by AHD's own griffin entry.

ref_check.note: FVQ_pages.txt leaf 92 (Jeffery p. 75), s.v. Baraka: 'To bless. ... The primitive verb b-r-k, which is not used in the Qur'an, means to kneel, used specially of the camel, so that baraka is the technical word for making a camel kneel. In this primitive sense it is common Semitic ... It was in the N. Semitic area, however, that the root seems to have developed the sense of to bless, and from thence it passed to the S. Semitic area. Thus we have Heb. bērēk, and Phon. brk to bless; Aram. brk to bless or praise; Syr. barrek ... From this N. Semitic sense we find derived the Sab. brk, Eth. bāraka to bless, celebrate the praises of, and Ar. bāraka as above.' — exactly Nourai's 'kneel (of the camel) → bless' story.

nodes.derivation: Arabic root b-r-k: baraka 'to kneel (of a camel)' (verbal noun burūk), Form III bāraka 'to bless', Form II barraka, Form VI tabāraka 'be blessed'; the noun baraka(t) 'blessing, divine favour' is the maṣdar-type noun of the root, with tāʾ marbūṭa -at (hence the transliteration barakat). Cognate with Hebrew bērēkh 'to bless' / bərākhā 'blessing'. Wiktionary lists 11 Arabic derivatives of the root.

ref_check.note: KLN_1966.txt leaf 98 (printed pp. ~160-164), s.v. 'berakah': 'Heb. berākhāh, blessing, from the stem of bērākh, he blessed, which is rel. to Aram. bārākh, Arab. bāraka, Ethiop. bārāka, he blessed, Akkad. karābu (a metathesis form), to bless, Ethiop. mekrab (metath.), temple. Cp. cherub, griffin.' Gives Arab. bāraka 'he blessed' under the Semitic root and the Akkadian metathesis, as the chart does.
Same page as the root: 'Ar. bāraka as above' derived from the N. Semitic sense 'to bless' (FVQ_pages.txt leaf 92).

nodes.derivation: New Persian barakat برکت is a direct loan of Arabic baraka(t) with the Arabic construct/pausal -at preserved as -at (a regular treatment of Arabic feminine nouns in Persian, cf. رحمت, نعمت); Wiktionary derives Urdu barkat from Classical Persian barakat < Arabic. The extra forms are all Arabic derivatives of the same root borrowed into Persian: tabrīk تبریک (Form II maṣdar 'congratulation'), tabarruk تبرّک (Form V maṣdar 'seeking blessing; blessed object'), mubārak مبارک (Form III passive participle 'blessed').

ref_check.note: FVA (Nahvi, Farhang-e vazheha-ye arabi dar farsi) has no digital copy (refs_online.json).

nodes.derivation: Akkadian karābu 'to pray, bless, greet, praise' (participle kāribu 'one who blesses/intercedes', diminutive kurību, a protective genius) is a real word of root k-r-b. Its connection to b-r-k is the metathesis hypothesis (Dhorme; Klein 164; AHD Semitic roots: 'krb, to praise, common Semitic root, with West Semitic metathesized variant brk'). So Nourai's cited sources (KLN, AHD) do assert this, and AHD still does; but the Semantics of Ancient Hebrew Database (Mitchell) rejects it because metathesis of the first and third radicals is extremely rare, and Wiktionary's Proto-Semitic *birk- page lists no Akkadian karābu. Verdict: accepted by some, rejected by others.

ref_check.note: KLN_1966.txt leaf 98 (printed pp. ~160-164), s.v. 'berakah': 'Heb. berākhāh, blessing, from the stem of bērākh, he blessed, which is rel. to Aram. bārākh, Arab. bāraka, Ethiop. bārāka, he blessed, Akkad. karābu (a metathesis form), to bless, Ethiop. mekrab (metath.), temple. Cp. cherub, griffin.' Klein calls Akkad. karābu 'a metathesis form' of b-r-k — Nourai's 'letters are interchanged'.

AHD:579 is the 1976 dictionary page (griffin); the current AHD griffin entry (archived, https://ahdictionary.com/word/search.html?q=griffin) derives griffin only 'from Greek grūps' with no Semitic link, but the AHD Semitic-roots appendix (archived, https://ahdictionary.com/word/semitic.html) s.v. krb: 'Common Semitic root, with West Semitic metathesized variant brk. cherub, from Hebrew kərûb, cherub; akin to Akkadian karābu, to praise, bless. Compare also brk' and s.v. brk: 'West Semitic, to bless. Probably a metathesized variant of krb.' — so AHD supports the Akkadian karābu ~ brk metathesis.

nodes.derivation: bərākhā בְּרָכָה 'blessing' (root b-r-k, verb bērēkh 'to bless', berekh 'knee') is a straightforward member of the root and is confirmed (cognate with Arabic baraka). kərūḇ כְּרוּב 'cherub' (pl. kərūḇīm; Gen. 3:24, Ex. 25:18) is by the mainstream view a loan from Akkadian kāribu/kurību 'intercessor; protective winged genius' (root k-r-b, karābu 'to bless') — so it belongs with Akkadian karābu (node 3), and the chart's placing of it under b-r-k stands or falls with the krb/brk metathesis hypothesis: endorsed by Klein and AHD, rejected by SAHD/Mitchell. Robert Alter's alternative ('hybrid' or, by consonant inversion, rkb 'mount/steed') is also on the table. Worst verdict for the node: plausible.

nodes.derivation: Arabic karūbī كَرُوبِيّ 'cherub, archangel' (pl. karūbiyyūn, as in al-malāʾika al-karūbiyyūn) is, per Wiktionary, borrowed from Hebrew kərūḇ (in practice through Jewish Aramaic/Syriac kərūḇā, the vehicle of most biblical vocabulary into Arabic) with the Arabic nisba suffix -iyy added to form an adjective/noun of relation; the word appears in early Islamic tradition (hadith and tafsīr) for the highest angels. Not from the Akkadian directly.

ref_check.note: vajehyab.com (Mo'in) s.v. کروبی: '(کَ یّ) [ع.] (اِ.) فرشتة مقرب درگاه. ج. کروبیون' — tagged Arabic; Mo'in's page numbers cannot be mapped online. Archived https://vajehyab.com/?q=کروبی&d=moein.

nodes.derivation: Persian karrūbī کرّوبی is Arabic karūbī taken over unchanged (Persian writers often geminate the r, karrūbī, as Nourai's spelling shows); the plurals karrūbiyān کروبیان (Persian -ān) and karrūbiyūn کروبیون (Arabic sound plural) are both used. Attested in classical poetry, e.g. Sa'di's Bustan (13th c.), as quoted in the chart. Gloss 'angel' is loose: the word means specifically 'cherub, one of the highest angels'. Nourai's source MON (Mo'in) is the standard Persian dictionary for this and Wiktionary's Arabic entry confirms the Arabic base; no independent Persian etymological page was found, but the Arabic loan is uncontroversial.

ref_check.note: vajehyab.com (Mo'in) s.v. کروبی [ع.] 'فرشتة مقرب درگاه، ج. کروبیون'; also کروبیان 'فرشتگان مقرب درگاه' and کروبیون 'جِ کروبی' — the Persian word is marked as an Arabic loan, as the arrow says (archived https://vajehyab.com/?q=کروبی&d=moein).

nodes.derivation: Hebrew kərūḇ was transliterated in the Septuagint (3rd–2nd c. BCE) as Greek χερούβ (pl. χερουβίμ), taken into Late Latin as cherub (pl. cherubim, Vulgate), and borrowed into Middle English in the late 14th c. as cherub 'an order of angels'; the sense 'winged child, putto' (the '(of love)' in Nourai's gloss) is Renaissance art usage, in English from c. 1705. The chart correctly draws it from Hebrew, not through Arabic. AHD's entry: 'from Late Latin, from Hebrew kərûb; see krb'.

ref_check.note: AHD online s.v. cherub (archived, https://ahdictionary.com/word/search.html?q=cherub): '[Middle English, from Late Latin, from Hebrew kərûb; see krb in the Appendix of Semitic roots.]' — Hebrew → (Latin →) English as in the chart; AHD:231 is the 1976 page of this entry.

nodes.derivation: Greek γρύψ grȳps, gen. γρυπός grȳpós 'griffin' (Herodotus, Aeschylus) — the second form Nourai gives, 'gruphos', is not a Greek nominative but reflects the genitive grypos / Latin gryphus. Its origin is unsettled: one view links it to γρυπός 'hook-nosed, curved' (PIE *ger- 'to bend'); Klein (KLN:680, Nourai's source) and Beekes allow a Pre-Greek/Anatolian loan ultimately from Semitic (Akkadian karūbu/kāribu, Hebrew kərūḇ) 'through the medium of the Hittites', making it a doublet of χερούβ. Wiktionary reports both; AHD's own griffin entry gives no Semitic source, and SAHD notes Brown's kərūḇ–γρύψ link 'finds minimal scholarly acceptance'. So the edge Hebrew kerubh → Greek gryps is a respectable but minority hypothesis.

ref_check.note: KLN_1966.txt leaf 367 (printed p. 681), s.v. 'griffin, griffon, gryphon': 'ME. griffon, fr. OF. grifoun (F. griffon), fr. Late L. gryphus ..., fr. Gk. grūps, gen. grūpos, which was prob. borrowed from the Semites through the medium of the Hittites. Cp. Heb. kerūbh, a winged angel, Akkad. karibu, epithet of the bull-colossus, lit. one who blesses, and see cherub.' — Klein does derive Gk. grūps from the Semitic kerūbh/karibu word (via Hittite), Nourai's arrow.

AHD online s.v. griffin (archived, https://ahdictionary.com/word/search.html?q=griffin): '[Middle English griffoun, from Old French griffon, from grif, from Latin grȳpus, grȳphus, variants of grȳps, grȳp-, from Greek grūps.]' — the chain below Greek is there, but AHD does not derive Greek grūps from Hebrew kerūbh; the Semitic appendix s.v. krb lists only cherub.

nodes.derivation: Latin grȳps, grȳpis (Vergil, Pliny) was borrowed from Greek γρύψ; Late Latin created the thematic variants grȳpus and grȳphus (the -ph- is a hypercorrect spelling, etymonline: 'misspelling of grypus'), and it is the Late Latin gryphus/grifus that the Romance forms continue.

ref_check.note: AHD online s.v. griffin (archived, https://ahdictionary.com/word/search.html?q=griffin): 'from Latin grȳpus, grȳphus, variants of grȳps, grȳp-, from Greek grūps' — Latin gryphus from Greek.

nodes.derivation: Old French grifon / griffon (12th c.; Anglo-Norman grifun, griffoun) is Late Latin gryphus with the augmentative/derivational suffix -on (< Latin -ōnem), i.e. from a Late Latin *grifonem; AHD: 'Old French griffon, from grif, from Latin grypus, gryphus'. The edge Latin → Old French → English is certain. The spelling 'grifion' printed here is not a standard attested Old French form (expected grifon/griffon); it may be Nourai's or the scan's slip for grifon, but since Klein's page could not be checked it is left as plausible rather than transcription_suspect.

ref_check.note: KLN_1966.txt leaf 367 (printed p. 681), s.v. 'griffin, griffon, gryphon': 'ME. griffon, fr. OF. grifoun (F. griffon), fr. Late L. gryphus ..., fr. Gk. grūps, gen. grūpos, which was prob. borrowed from the Semites through the medium of the Hittites. Cp. Heb. kerūbh, a winged angel, Akkad. karibu, epithet of the bull-colossus, lit. one who blesses, and see cherub.' Klein: 'ME. griffon, fr. OF. grifoun (F. griffon), fr. Late L. gryphus' — OF from Latin; the OF spelling grifion in the chart is Nourai's/OCR's.

nodes.derivation: Middle English griffoun, griffon (c. 1200 as a surname, 14th c. as the beast) from Old French grifon; the modern spelling griffin/gryphon settled in the 16th–17th c. (gryphon re-Latinised after Latin gryphus). Sense: the eagle-headed, lion-bodied guardian of Scythian gold in Greek legend.

entries.modern_form: Proto-Semitic *baraḳ- 'lightning', root b-r-q 'to flash, shine' (AHD Semitic roots brq)
entries.note: Root, label and gloss are correct: Wiktionary reconstructs Proto-Semitic *baraḳ- 'lightning' (Akk. birqum, Heb. bārāq, Aram. barqā, Ar. barq, Ge'ez bärḳ), from Proto-Afroasiatic *bǐrk'-/*bǎrk'- 'to flash'; AHD Semitic appendix brq 'to flash (especially of lightning)' with emerald as its English derivative. The emerald branch (Semitic barraqtu/bāreqet → Greek smaragdos → Latin → Romance/English; Greek → Iranian/Arabic zumurrud) is standard (AHD, etymonline, Beekes, Noonan 2012). Two problems in this chart: the Greek form is misprinted/misread ('smaraldos' for smaragdos), and the Arabic → Persian direction for zumurrud is reversed relative to Wiktionary/MacKenzie (Middle Persian uzumburd is pre-Islamic).

ref_check.note: KLN_1966.txt leaf 280 (printed pp. 514-515), s.v. 'emerald': 'ME. emeraude, fr. OF. esmeralde, esmeraude (F. émeraude), fr. L. smaragdus (whence also It. smeraldo, Sp. esmeralda), fr. Gk. smaragdos, maragdos, emerald, which is of Sem. origin. Cp. Heb. bāreqeth, Akkad. barraqtu, emerald, lit. something flashing, a derivative of Heb. bārāq, resp. Akkad. birqu, lightning, which are rel. to Aram. beraq, barqā, Arab. barq, lightning, Heb. bāraq, Aram. beraq, Arab. baraqa, Ethiop. baraqa, it flashed, glistened, Akkad. barāqu, to flash. Cp. OI. marakatam, Pers. zumurrud (whence Turk. zümrüd, whence Russ. izumrud), emerald, which are also Sem. loan words. Cp. also smaragd, which is a doublet of emerald.' Klein gives the whole Semitic b-r-q 'flash, lightning' family under 'emerald'.

nodes.derivation: Arabic root b-r-q: baraqa 'to flash (of lightning), shine, glitter', noun barq 'lightning' (Qur'an 2:19–20 yakādu l-barqu yakhṭafu abṣārahum); Wiktionary: from Proto-Semitic *baraḳ-, noting the Arabic noun may be a deverbal formation rather than a direct inheritance. Derivatives barrāq 'glittering' (intensive faʿʿāl), bāriqa 'flash' (active participle).

nodes.derivation: Persian barq برق is borrowed from Arabic barq 'lightning' (Wiktionary: 'Persian borrowed the term directly from Arabic'); attested in Ferdowsi's Shahnameh (c. 1000 CE) in the sense 'lightning', as the chart's quotation shows. The sense 'electricity' is a 19th–20th-c. semantic extension in Persian (cf. barqī 'electric', barq-kār 'electrician'), paralleled by Arabic barq 'telegraph'. The extras barrāq برّاق 'glittering' and bāriqa بارقه 'flash, gleam' are further Arabic derivatives of the root borrowed into Persian.

nodes.derivation: The Akkadian word for 'lightning' is birqu (Proto-Semitic *baraḳ-, Wiktionary lists Akkadian birqum); the form Nourai prints, baraqtu, corresponds to Neo-Babylonian barraqtu 'emerald, a flashing green stone' (AHD: 'akin to Akkadian barraqtu and Hebrew bāreqet, a kind of gemstone (probably emerald)'), a -t- derivative of barāqu 'to flash'. So the word is real and belongs to this root (KLN:514 s.v. emerald cites it), but the gloss 'lightning' is a conflation: barraqtu is the gem-name, and it is precisely the form from which Greek smaragdos is derived, so it ought to sit as the parent of the Greek node rather than as a sister.

Klein has Akkad. barraqtu but glosses it 'emerald, lit. something flashing' (a derivative of Akkad. birqu 'lightning'); Nourai's gloss 'lightning' belongs to birqu, not to baraqtu.

nodes.derivation: The Greek word is σμάραγδος smáragdos (also μάραγδος máragdos), 'emerald, green gem' (Herodotus, Theophrastus; Marcus Aurelius); 'smaraldos' with -ld- is not a Greek form and is almost certainly a misreading of the -gd- cluster (gd → ld) in the scan, since Klein (KLN:514) prints smaragdos. Etymology as drawn is confirmed: Wiktionary, AHD, etymonline and Beekes derive smaragdos from a Semitic source, Akkadian barraqtu / Hebrew bāreqet (Ex. 28:17) 'flashing gem', root b-r-q; the initial s- and the -agd- are the Greek adaptation of the Semitic b-r-q-t cluster (Noonan 2012 on Northwest Semitic loanwords). Old Armenian zmruxt also stems from it.

nodes.derivation: Pass-through node: Arabic zumurrud زُمُرُّد 'emerald' does go back to Greek smaragdos, but not directly: Wiktionary derives Arabic zumurrud from Persian zumurrud (< Middle Persian ʾwzmbwlt /uzumburd/ < Greek), i.e. Persian is the intermediary into Arabic rather than the reverse; another route often cited is Syriac zmaragdā. Arabic zabarjad 'peridot' is a doublet. The chart's Greek → Arabic → Persian ordering reverses the direction Wiktionary/MacKenzie give, so the Arabic node's parent is right in substance (Greek origin) but its child edge is not.

Mo'in's tag [معر - یو.] = Arabicized (mu'arrab) from Greek, i.e. Greek → Arabic → Persian, which is the route drawn through this empty Arabic node. Archived https://vajehyab.com/?q=زمرد&d=moein.

nodes.derivation: Persian zumurrud/zomorrod زمرّد 'emerald' is, per Wiktionary, inherited from Middle Persian uzumburd (Book Pahlavi ʾwzmbwlt), itself borrowed from Greek σμάραγδος in the Sasanian period; the prothetic u-/i- (cf. Early New Persian uzmurud, Russian izumrud, Turkish zümrüt) reflects the un-Persian initial cluster sm- (s- > z- by voicing before m, -gd- > -rd/-rrd). Arabic zumurrud is then a loan FROM Persian (Wiktionary), not its source; etymonline likewise gives Persian zumurrud as the source of Turkish and Russian without an Arabic step. Modern sources therefore reverse the chart's Arabic → Persian edge; the ultimate origin (Semitic b-r-q via Greek), which KLN:514 also gives, is not in doubt.

nodes.derivation: Latin smaragdus (m./f.), Pliny, Vulgate — a direct borrowing of Greek σμάραγδος with Greek -os rendered by the Latin 2nd-declension -us. In Vulgar/Medieval Latin it became smaralda, smaraldus, esmaraldus (with -gd- > -ld- by dissimilation and a prothetic e- before the s+consonant cluster), the source of all Romance forms.

nodes.derivation: smaragdite 'a green foliated amphibole found in eclogite/gabbro' is a learned mineralogical coinage (French smaragdite, H.-B. de Saussure, 1796) from Latin smaragdus + the mineral suffix -ite (< Greek -ītēs), named for its emerald-green colour; English from French in the early 19th c. The Latin → English edge is via scientific French, with no Old French step.

ref_check.note: AHD:427 is the 1976 page of 'emerald'; the current AHD emerald entry (archived, https://ahdictionary.com/word/search.html?q=emerald) reads '[Middle English emeraude, from Old French, from Medieval Latin esmeralda, esmeraldus, from Latin smaragdus, from Greek smaragdos; akin to Sanskrit marakatam, probably of Semitic origin; akin to Akkadian barraqtu and Hebrew bāreqet, a kind of gemstone ...; see brq in the Appendix of Semitic roots.]' — it confirms Latin smaragdus < Greek but does not treat smaragdite (the AHD search for smaragdite, archived https://ahdictionary.com/word/search.html?q=smaragdite, returned no entry). Klein (KLN_1966.txt leaf 280-281 s.v. smaragdite): 'F., formed with subst. suff. -ite fr. Gk. smaragdos, emerald'.

nodes.derivation: Old French esmeraude (12th c.), with the variants esmeralde, esmeragde, smaralde listed by Wiktionary, from Vulgar Latin *smaralda/*smaraldus (< Latin smaragdus): prothetic e- before s+C, -gd- > -ld- > -ud- (vocalisation of l before a consonant gives the standard esmeraude), so esmeralde is the conservative form; Modern French émeraude.

nodes.derivation: Middle English emeraude (c. 1300) from Old French esmeraude; the modern spelling emerald with -ld restored (after Medieval Latin esmaraldus / Old French esmeralde) appears from the 15th–16th c. AHD: 'Middle English emeraude, from Old French, from Medieval Latin esmeralda, esmeraldus, from Latin smaragdus, from Greek smaragdos'.

ref_check.note: AHD online s.v. emerald (archived, https://ahdictionary.com/word/search.html?q=emerald): 'Middle English emeraude, from Old French, from Medieval Latin esmeralda, esmeraldus, from Latin smaragdus, from Greek smaragdos ... probably of Semitic origin; akin to Akkadian barraqtu and Hebrew bāreqet' — the whole chain of this branch, including the Semitic b-r-q root.

nodes.derivation: Sanskrit marakata (n.) 'emerald' (Pali marakata, Prakrit maragaya; hence Tamil marakatam, Thai morakot, Tibetan mar gad) is a genuine word and, as the chart implies, ultimately of Semitic origin; Wiktionary labels it 'from Semitic', linking it with Greek σμάραγδος. But the immediate source is debated: Noonan and the classicists (Chantraine, Beekes, Mayrhofer) treat marakata as a late loan from Greek smaragdos (loss of initial s-, -gd- > -k-t-), i.e. Greek rather than the Semitic root directly; older scholarship (still echoed in some sources) even took Sanskrit as the source of the Semitic words, which is now rejected. So 'from the Semitic root' is right in ultimate origin but the direct edge Semitic → Sanskrit is uncertain.
